title: The buffer pool: pin, dirty, LRU, and CLOCK
lead: Trace the state: which pages may be replaced, which must be written back, and why?
goals: Update pin counts and dirty flags correctly
Simulate LRU and CLOCK when some pages are pinned
Explain sequential flooding and the limits of replacement policies

sections.title: Request a page and protect its frame
sections.html:
A query needs page P. If P is already in RAM, the DBMS can use it immediately: this is a buffer hit. Otherwise, the DBMS must load P: this is a buffer miss. The buffer pool is the RAM area holding pages; each frame is a space that holds one page.

Pinning marks a page as in use; the pin count records outstanding uses that have not yet been released. Unpinning releases one use. Only a frame with pin count 0 may be selected for replacement, or eviction. A dirty page has been modified in RAM but not yet written back to disk. Its modified contents must be preserved under the required persistence protocol before eviction removes it from its frame.

A buffer request is a state transition

The page table maps page IDs to frames. On a hit, pin the resident frame. On a miss, take a free frame or choose an unpinned victim; preserve a dirty victim before replacing it. Read the incoming page into the frame, initially clean, and pin it. Every successful pin needs a matching unpin. These steps manage safe use of the frame; transaction correctness also needs concurrency control and recovery.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15 ↗. The worked examples are original.

sections.title: An original trace: pinning and dirty state
sections.html:
Initially P has pin=0 and dirty=false. Two users each call pin(P), increasing the counter by one each time: pin=2. The first user modifies the page and calls unpin(P,true): pin falls to 1 and dirty=true. The second user only reads and calls unpin(P,false): pin falls to 0, but dirty remains true.

Key takeaway

Pin count and the dirty flag answer different questions. Pin=0 means nobody still holds the page; dirty=true means there are changes not yet written to disk. Unpinning with false says only that this user made no modification. It does not erase an earlier user’s dirty state.

P is now eligible for replacement, but is not necessarily evicted immediately. If a cache miss selects P as its victim, the cost may include one write of P and one read of the incoming page. A pin count also does not by itself prevent conflicting writes; coordinating them requires concurrency control.

Check yourself: what if every frame is still pinned?

No frame is eligible for eviction. An implementation must wait, report that no frame is available, or use another management mechanism. It cannot ignore pin counts and overwrite an in-use page. This is an additional implementation inference from the invariant, a condition that must always hold.

sections.title: An original LRU trace: eight requests, three frames
sections.html:
Assume each request pins its page and immediately unpins it; all three frames start empty and every page is clean. The request trace is A,B,C,A,D,B,A,C. LRU (least recently used) records the most recent unpin, the end of use, in this lecture’s convention. It selects the eligible page whose last unpin is furthest in the past. Under this assumption, that is also the least recently used page.

  1. A,B,C: 3 misses; oldest→newest order is A,B,C.
  2. A: hit; B,C,A.
  3. D: miss, evict B; C,A,D.
  4. B: miss, evict C; A,D,B.
  5. A: hit; D,B,A.
  6. C: miss, evict D; B,A,C.

The result is 6 misses, 2 hits, and 0 write-backs. The first three misses fill empty frames; the next three replace B, C, and then D. If D is dirty when evicted, the miss count stays the same but one write is added.

Key takeaway

Count cache misses and write-backs separately. A miss means the requested page is absent from the pool. In this model, an extra write occurs only when a dirty page must be replaced; six misses do not mean six writes.

With A,B,C,D repeating through three LRU frames, every request misses: each cycle needs four pages, but only three fit, and the page needed next has already been evicted. This is sequential flooding. “Recently used” does not guarantee “needed again soon”.

sections.title: An original CLOCK trace and comparison exercise
sections.html:
CLOCK moves a hand around the frames. The reference bit, ref, records recent use and is set when the pin count increases in this lecture’s convention. When CLOCK encounters an unpinned page with ref=1, it clears the bit and gives the page another chance. Consider the ring F0,F1,F2 with the hand at F0. The frames contain A(pin=1,ref=1), B(pin=0,ref=1), and C(pin=0,ref=0), respectively. We need to load D.

  1. Skip A because it is pinned. Needing space does not make A eligible.
  2. At B, set ref to 0 and continue.
  3. At C, ref=0 and the page is unpinned, so select C.
  4. Load D into F2, set pin=1 and ref=1, and advance the hand to F0.

Practise by changing C.ref to 1. The hand skips A, clears B.ref and C.ref, then returns and skips A again. If no intervening access occurs, B is the first page encountered again with ref=0. Now compare CLOCK with MRU (most recently used), which replaces the most recently used eligible page, on the repeated scan below.

MRU can help a repeated scan under stated assumptions

Original trace with three frames, initially empty, clean pages, and immediate unpin after every request: A B C D A B C D. LRU misses on all eight requests. MRU first evicts C for D; A and B then hit, C misses and evicts B, and D hits. MRU therefore has five misses with victims C then B. This example does not make MRU universally best; a different working set and access pattern can reverse the comparison.

Exercise: what assumptions allow the MRU trace to evict C on request D?

Worked answer. A, B and C have all been unpinned immediately after use, so all are eligible. C is most recent. If C remained pinned, this victim choice would be invalid.

Preview: practical buffer choices

Maintaining detailed LRU recency has overhead; CLOCK approximates it with reference bits and a sweep. LRU-K uses a deeper history of page references. Systems may also partition budgets for data, indexes and logs, use priority hints, or prefetch expected pages. A wrong prefetch prediction can waste I/O and replace useful cached pages. Dirty-page writes must still respect the log-before-data rule of write-ahead logging (WAL), plus recovery and concurrency rules, developed later.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 22, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34 ↗. The worked examples are original.

quiz.question: P has dirty=true. What is dirty after unpin(P,false)?
options: It depends on the pin count
quiz.explanation: The new dirty flag is the old dirty flag OR the supplied dirty argument. true OR false remains true.
